posts.name: Dividendology
posts.text:
I recently interviewed Dwayne Hyzak, the CEO of Main Street Capital $MAIN-

Which is possibly the greatest monthly dividend paying stocks of all time.

Main Street makes money by providing both debt and equity capital to mature, owner-operated businesses in the lower middle market.

That earns it recurring interest income, plus a share of the upside when those companies grow.

This has led to susbstaintale outperformance since they went public.

And according to Dwayne, one of Main Street’s biggest advantages right now comes from what it does NOT own:

Software.

When I asked about Main Street’s software exposure, he said:

“If there’s an area, or a couple of areas, that we are underexposed to, one of those would be software.”

That’s by design.

Main Street focuses on basic, mature companies, businesses that have “been around for decades, not years.”

Then he added:

“We probably got criticized for not having more exposure to software historically. I think clearly today we view that as a strength and a benefit.”

Meanwhile, many other BDCs spent the last five years leaning into software-

A space that’s come under serious pressure over the last year, largely because of AI.

Now, according to Dwayne, those BDCs are shifting toward basic industrial businesses that “look and feel more like what Main Street has always invested in.”

When I asked whether AI has changed how Main Street underwrites deals, his answer was simple:

“We’re not big software guys, so it’s not like AI is going to fundamentally change the vast majority of the companies that we either invest in or that we look at.”

AI can help someone build competing software…

But it can’t recreate a manufacturer or distributor with decades of customer relationships behind it.

Sometimes the most “boring” businesses are the hardest to disrupt.

Dwayne and I also talked about Main Street’s dividend policy, how they decide on the supplemental dividend, why issuing shares above NAV can benefit shareholders, and where he sees the company 10 years from now.

$VLO $MPC $PSX $DK $CLMT RUSSIAN REFINERY RUNS DROP TO LOWEST IN DECADES, RYSTAD SAYS

THE ESTIMATE
• Rystad Energy puts Russian refinery runs at 2.6 to 2.7 million barrels a day as of Monday, roughly halving since Oct. 30 and the lowest in more than two decades
• Rystad calculates runs by monitoring crude-supply chains, tanker tracking, satellite images and industry sources
• The estimate does not include the impact of Wednesday's strikes on two refineries in the Samara region
• Bloomberg's tally counts at least 18 refineries attacked since late October, though not all of the nameplate capacity hit is necessarily affected

THE CROSS-CHECKS
• Rystad's own ladder: 5.0 million barrels a day in late October, 4.2 million over the first ten days of November, now 2.6 to 2.7 million. The decline accelerated hard in the last two weeks
• The Ukraine_Data oil tracker, an independent bottom-up model, put runs at a 3.37 million barrel a day mid estimate on Nov. 19, inside a 2.6 to 4.35 million band, with its own crisis threshold at 2.8 million. Rystad's range sits at the bottom of that band and below that threshold
• Two independent methodologies converge on the same zone: the direction is high confidence, the exact level is one firm's estimate
• Against late-October runs, the Rystad range implies roughly 45 to 50% of Russian throughput is now offline. The Samara exclusion cuts less than the headline suggests: both Samara plants were already effectively offline, so Wednesday's strikes extend outages rather than removing running barrels

THE OFFICIAL SIGNAL
• President Putin said on Tuesday the situation on the domestic oil-product market "remains challenging"; Deputy Prime Minister Novak said on Wednesday the situation is "quite tense" (Tass)
• Average weekly retail gasoline prices rose 0.5% in the Nov. 17-23 period, the biggest weekly increase since early September (Federal Statistics Service)
• Gasoline and jet fuel export restrictions remain in place, fuel imports continue, and diesel supplies to global markets have been allowed only following an agreement with the US

THE MARKET SPLIT
• Crude Moscow cannot process is being diverted into the export stream, lifting overseas crude sales and adding to the global crude surplus
• The tight leg is products: Russian diesel, gasoline and jet supply is short, which supports product cracks into Europe and US Gulf Coast export arbs
• The offset in the US is a soft domestic print run: two straight EIA distillate builds, with the industry survey pointing to a third in the week just ended, and the front 3-2-1 crack printing 37.60 on Nov. 24
• Watch: the next Ukraine_Data tracker print against its 2.8 million barrel a day crisis line, Russian diesel export loadings, and any rationing or regional shortage headlines

Zscaler is a leader in network security, which CrowdStrike calls cyber's largest single market.
 
After close, Falcon covers the device an agent runs on and the network it connects through.
 
CrowdStrike says the deal adds $185B+ to its addressable market in 2029.
 
Zscaler had struggled with go-to-market, something CrowdStrike excels at.
 
While many view the $500M of cost and ~$1B of revenue synergies as aggressive, they may prove to be conservative.
 
CrowdStrike is buying Zscaler at 11.3x ARR, paying with its own stock valued at ~37x ARR.

3️⃣ Palo Alto is making another bold move to expand into AI models with its $4.5B offer for Applied Compute.

After CyberArk, Palo Alto already covers most of the cybersecurity map.
 
Applied Compute isn't on it. It helps enterprises train and run their own open-weight models.

Enterprises want more control over their AI models, but they also need to trust them in production.
 
Pairing Applied Compute’s model-training team with Palo Alto’s security expertise could help address both needs.

The Nasdaq-100 is cheaper on forward earnings today than it was at the bottom of the dot-com crash.

That 57% is coming from a tiny group of early users. As adoption increases, which it inevitably will, the volume will explode beyond anything we can comprehend.

And every one of those agents has to pay for things. Data, compute, the work of other agents, often a cent or less at a time. All of that will happen onchain.

That changes the maths on crypto completely. Every adoption forecast added up the humans who might one day use it. But humans are about to be the minority of users, the same way they're already the minority of the internet...

posts.text: The tariff headline that hit the tape on yesterday deserves more than a line, because it is not a tweet, it is a process. The administration is preparing findings from a Section 301 probe into excess industrial capacity across 16 trading partners, with rates up to 20% on China, 15% on the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, and higher still on Vietnam and India. The tariffs could begin in January after hearings, and the US-China truce expires Jan 10, so the calendar is tight. Asia's chip names sold off hard on it, and the US tape followed. The market's fear is not the tariff itself, it is the second-order effect: tariffs on industrial capacity mean higher input costs for the same companies building the AI data centers, and slower global growth while the Fed is hiking. The probe is a process with hearings, which means headlines will keep coming. The trade is not to guess the outcome, it is to know the dates: hearings, January, Jan 10.

posts.text: The bond market disagreed with the inflation print on yesterday , and the bond market is usually the one worth listening to. Core PCE came in a tenth hot, GDP was revised up to a strong number, and the 10-year yield fell anyway, down more than 9 basis points to around 4.81%. Yields fall when the market fears growth more than inflation, and that is the read. The tape sold off on tariff headlines, not on the inflation number, and the bond market said the hiking path is already priced. A December hike is the base case and everyone knows it. What the bond market is pricing now is what comes after: a Fed that hikes into a slowing economy because it has to, not because it wants to. When yields fall on a hot print, the market is telling you the growth scare is the bigger story. Watch the 10-year into Friday. If it keeps falling while stocks bounce, the bond market is calling the recovery a relief rally. If yields stabilize, the growth fear is passing.

posts.name: Joseph Brusuelas
posts.text:
Want to wish everyone an early Happy Thanksgiving and traditional holiday season.  

Through the end of the year there will be a focus on food and gift prices that are rising. 

Given the successive price shocks over the past five years that makes perfect sense. 

While I understand it's all too easy to look at the $35 Thanksgiving meal with all the trimmings that feeds 10 from Wal-Mart and project wonder about their profitable supply chain, I think it is missing the point. 
 
It’s the little things that we all do around this time. 
 
The handmade sage sausage in the stuffing. The grated orange in the cranberry sauce. The wine infusion in the turkey. The handwritten note for Christmas. 

That is what really matters at the holidays.

The $35 all in via Wal-Mart may appeal to many but I think it angers the majority.

Why?

Because too many households feel pushed into purchasing it due to rising cost of living. 

For those that would put forward solutions to the affordability challenges that sit before the American economy it is something to remember. 

What on the surface appears to be a bargain-that permits many to take part in a way they can't due to economic reasons- it's a not so gentle reminder of our own shortcomings and a type of market failure that all too many will never admit.

So when one looks at sour public attitudes around the economy or rising public inflation expectations it’s the little things in the aggregate that we all too often miss that are the cause of such discontent.

Be creative, innovative and don't be afraid to turn over a table or two of self-important VIP's to restore a semblance  of economic security and price stability. 

As our good friends @nytimes  use  to remind us within the black and white newsprint of an age gone by: 

Remember the neediest at the holidays.

Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans https://cnb.cx/4jBQWiT
